title: Tobit
language: Aramaic or Hebrew original (fragments of four Aramaic copies and one Hebrew copy found at Qumran, 4Q196-200); survives complete in two Greek forms (short and long) and in Latin.
origin: A Jewish author, probably in the Diaspora (eastern Mediterranean or Mesopotamia) or possibly Judea; the story is set among Israelite exiles in Nineveh after 722 BC.
summary:
Tobit is a short, carefully told family story. Tobit, a devout Israelite of the tribe of Naphtali deported to Nineveh, buries executed fellow Jews at the risk of his life, is blinded by bird droppings and prays to die. Far away in Ecbatana, a young relative named Sarah has lost seven husbands on their wedding nights to the demon Asmodeus and also prays to die. God sends the angel Raphael, disguised as a kinsman, to guide Tobit's son Tobias on a journey: a fish caught in the Tigris yields the cure for both troubles, Tobias marries Sarah, and Tobit's sight is restored.

The book is a showcase of Diaspora piety: almsgiving, prayer, fasting, burial of the dead, marrying within one's people, honouring parents and keeping faith far from Jerusalem. Tobit's farewell speeches (chapters 4 and 14) contain a negative form of the Golden Rule and the hope that Jerusalem and the Temple will be rebuilt in glory. Historians note that the story compresses or confuses some Assyrian history (for example it makes Sennacherib the son of Shalmaneser, when his father was Sargon II, and has Tobit alive from the division of the kingdom to the fall of Nineveh). Many readers, Catholic scholars included, therefore read it as an edifying tale rather than a chronicle.
plain: A family story about a blind, faithful Jew in exile, his son's journey with a disguised angel, and a bride freed from a demon. It teaches prayer, generosity and trust in God's hidden care. Catholics and Orthodox count it as Scripture; Jews and most Protestants do not.
contents: Tobit's good deeds and blindness in Nineveh (ch. 1-3)
Sarah's plight in Ecbatana and the two prayers heard together (ch. 3)
Tobit's instructions to his son, including almsgiving and the negative Golden Rule (ch. 4)
Journey with Raphael, the fish, marriage to Sarah and the demon driven off (ch. 5-9)
Homecoming and healing of Tobit's eyes; Raphael reveals himself as one of seven angels (ch. 10-12)
Tobit's hymn and final prophecy of a rebuilt Jerusalem (ch. 13-14)
whyRejected:
Jews: Tobit was never part of the Hebrew Bible. Rabbinic tradition held that the books defiling the hands (that is, sacred) were closed, and Tobit circulated mainly in Greek. The Qumran finds show Jews did read it in Aramaic and Hebrew before AD 70, so the exclusion was not because no Semitic original existed.

Protestants: the Reformers followed Jerome's *Hebraica veritas* (Hebrew truth) principle: the Old Testament canon is the Hebrew Bible the Jews kept. They also pointed to historical difficulties (the Assyrian king list, Tobit's improbable life span), to Raphael's fish-liver smoke against a demon (which seemed magical to them), and to the teaching that almsgiving purges sin (Tob 12:9), which they saw as clashing with justification by faith. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles lets it be read for example of life but not for doctrine; the Westminster Confession gives it no authority.
whyValued:
Catholics and Orthodox note that Tobit was in the Greek Old Testament used by most early Christians, was read and cited by Fathers such as Polycarp, Cyprian and Augustine, and appears in the lists of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397). Trent (1546) and Jerusalem (1672) confirmed it. The Ethiopian and Syriac churches also keep it.

Its defenders value it as a theology of everyday faithfulness: God works through ordinary events and hidden angels, prayer is answered, marriage is holy (Tobias's wedding-night prayer is still read at Catholic weddings), and charity matters. Raphael's statement that he is one of seven angels who stand before God is echoed in Revelation, and almsgiving language resembles that of Jesus. On the historical slips, Catholic scholars often answer that the book's genre is a didactic story, so its truth does not depend on Assyrian chronology.

Its piety is fully Jewish and mostly uncontroversial; Protestants object to almsgiving that purges sin (Tob 12:9) and the angelic exorcism.

title: Judith
language: Probably a Hebrew original (the Greek is full of Hebrew idioms) now lost; survives in Greek; Jerome made his Latin from an Aramaic copy.
origin: A Jewish author in Judea, probably in the Hasmonean (Maccabean) period, telling a story set in an imaginary Israel threatened by an Assyrian army.
summary:
Judith is a dramatic tale of national deliverance. The army of Holofernes, general of Nebuchadnezzar, besieges the hill town of Bethulia, which guards the way to Jerusalem. As the water runs out the elders agree to surrender in five days. Judith, a wealthy, devout widow, rebukes them for testing God, prays, dresses in her finery and goes into the enemy camp. She wins Holofernes' trust, and when he lies drunk in his tent she cuts off his head with his own sword. The leaderless army panics and flees, and Judith leads Israel in a victory song.

The book opens with what look like deliberate impossibilities: Nebuchadnezzar is called king of the Assyrians ruling in Nineveh (Nineveh fell in 612 BC, before his reign), the Temple has recently been rededicated after the return from exile, and Bethulia is otherwise unknown. Many modern scholars, including Catholic ones, read these as signals that the story is a theological novella, a composite of Israel's enemies, not a botched history. Others in older Catholic and Orthodox writing tried to fit it into real history (for example under Ashurbanipal or Artaxerxes III). Its themes echo Jael and Deborah, the Exodus song and the Maccabean struggle.
plain: A story about a brave, prayerful widow who saves her town by beheading an enemy general. It celebrates God rescuing his people through the weak. Catholics and Orthodox count it as Scripture; Jews and Protestants do not, partly because its history does not line up with what we know.

Israel prepares; Achior the Ammonite warns Holofernes that Israel is protected while faithful (ch. 4-6)
Siege of Bethulia and the elders' five-day deadline (ch. 7)
Judith's rebuke, prayer and plan (ch. 8-9)
Judith in the enemy camp and the beheading of Holofernes (ch. 10-13)
Rout of the Assyrians and Judith's song of praise (ch. 14-16)
whyRejected:
Jews: not part of the Hebrew Bible; no Hebrew text survived in Jewish use, though medieval Hebrew retellings tied it to Hanukkah. Some scholars suggest that its Hasmonean flavour or the conversion of Achior (an Ammonite, compare Deut 23:3) made it awkward, but the main reason is simply that it was outside the received collection.

Protestants: Luther found it edifying but suggested it was a sacred drama or allegory rather than history. The Reformers applied Jerome's Hebrew-canon rule and pointed to the apparent historical errors (Nebuchadnezzar as king of Assyria in Nineveh, unknown places, a garbled chronology) as evidence it was not inspired history. Some also objected to Judith's deceptive words to Holofernes being praised. Article VI lists it as readable for example but not doctrine.
whyValued:
Catholic and Orthodox churches received it from the Greek Old Testament. Clement of Rome held Judith up as an example of courageous faith before AD 100, and Jerome reported that the Council of Nicaea was said to have counted it among the Scriptures (which is why he translated it despite doubts). Hippo, Carthage, Trent and Jerusalem 1672 list it.

Defenders say it should be judged as the kind of writing it is: an inspired story whose truth is theological. It teaches that God saves by the hand of a woman (Jdt 9:10; 13:15), that leaders must not put God on a deadline, and that prayer, fasting and courage go together. Judith became a model of Israel itself and, for many Fathers, a figure of the Church and of Mary.

title: Additions to Esther

alternatives.label: Colophon dated to 114 BC (Ptolemy VIII and Cleopatra III)
Colophon dated to 78/77 BC (Ptolemy XII and Cleopatra V)

language: Greek; two additions (the royal decrees B and E) were composed in polished Greek, while others (A, C, D, F) may go back to Hebrew or Aramaic sources.
origin: Jewish translators and editors; a colophon says the Greek Esther was brought to Egypt by Dositheus and translated by Lysimachus son of Ptolemy of Jerusalem.
summary:
The Greek version of Esther contains six blocks of material (107 verses), usually labelled A to F, that are not in the Hebrew book. A opens with Mordecai's dream of two dragons and his uncovering of a plot; B gives the text of Haman's decree to destroy the Jews; C contains long prayers of Mordecai and Esther; D expands Esther's unsummoned approach to the king, who softens when God changes his spirit; E is the king's second decree, condemning Haman; F interprets the dream and ends with a colophon about the translation.

The most striking effect is religious. The Hebrew Esther famously never names God, while the additions mention God over fifty times, add prayer, and have Esther protest that she loathes the pagan marriage bed and has not eaten at Haman's table. Jerome, translating from Hebrew, moved the additions to the end of his book, which is why Catholic Bibles once numbered them as Esther 10:4-16:24; modern Catholic Bibles put them back in their story order with letters.
plain: Extra passages found in the Greek version of Esther, adding prayers, dreams and royal letters. They make the story openly religious, since the Hebrew Esther never mentions God. Catholics and Orthodox read them as part of Esther; Jews and Protestants follow the shorter Hebrew book.
contents: A: Mordecai's dream of two dragons and the eunuchs' plot (before Esth 1:1)
B: Text of the king's decree against the Jews (after Esth 3:13)
C: Prayers of Mordecai and Esther (after Esth 4:17)
D: Esther before the king; God changes his anger to gentleness (replacing Esth 5:1-2)
E: The king's decree in favour of the Jews (after Esth 8:12)
F: The dream explained and the translation colophon (after Esth 10:3)
whyRejected:
Jews keep the Hebrew Esther, read at Purim, without these passages; they were never part of the Hebrew text.

Protestants followed Jerome, who marked them as additions found only in Greek. Since no Hebrew original was known and the decrees are plainly Greek compositions, Reformers treated them as secondary expansions. Some also noted inconsistencies with the Hebrew story (for example Haman is called a Macedonian in Addition E, and the timing of Mordecai's reward differs). Article VI lists the rest of Esther among books read but not used for doctrine.

Syriac: the Peshitta Esther follows the Hebrew and lacks the additions, hence n/a.
whyValued: Catholic and Orthodox churches received Esther in its Greek form as part of the Septuagint, and Trent defined the books with all their parts as they were read in the Church. For them, the additions are an inspired interpretation that makes explicit what the Hebrew leaves implicit: that God guided events and that Esther's courage rose from prayer. Esther's prayer (Addition C) has long been used in Christian devotion and liturgy. The Ethiopian tradition likewise uses the fuller Esther.

title: Wisdom of Solomon
language: Greek, written in Greek from the start (it uses Greek rhetorical forms and philosophical terms).
origin: A learned Jew in Alexandria, Egypt, writing in the voice of King Solomon (a literary convention, not a claim most readers took literally; Jerome and Augustine knew it was not by Solomon).
summary:
Wisdom is a sustained appeal, written in the persona of Solomon, to love righteousness and seek divine Wisdom. Part one contrasts the ungodly, who think life ends at death and so oppress the righteous, with the righteous whose souls are in the hand of God and who will shine in judgement. Part two praises Wisdom herself as a breath of God's power, a pure emanation of his glory, a reflection of eternal light, and recounts Solomon's prayer for her. Part three retells the Exodus as a lesson in how God uses creation to punish the wicked and rescue the righteous, with a long critique of idolatry.

Wisdom is a bridge text. It is thoroughly Jewish yet uses Greek ideas such as the immortality of the soul and the four cardinal virtues. Its language about Wisdom and its argument that idolatry leads to immorality closely resemble passages in Paul, Hebrews and John, so many scholars think New Testament writers knew it, though none quotes it by name.
plain: A Greek-Jewish book written in Solomon's name that praises God's Wisdom, promises immortality to the righteous and mocks idol-worship. Its ideas sound very like parts of Paul and Hebrews. Catholics and Orthodox count it as Scripture; Jews and Protestants do not.
contents: The fate of the righteous and the ungodly; immortality (ch. 1-5)
Solomon's search for Wisdom and portrait of Wisdom (ch. 6-9)
Wisdom's work in history from Adam to the Exodus (ch. 10)
The Exodus plagues as measured judgement and mercy (ch. 11-12, 16-19)
The folly and origins of idolatry (ch. 13-15)
whyRejected:
Jews: composed in Greek in Egypt and never part of the Hebrew Bible; the rabbis did not transmit it.

Protestants: the Reformers accepted Jerome's judgement that it was not by Solomon and not in the Hebrew canon, so it could not be prophetic Scripture. Luther admired it but noted its late Greek origin. Article VI places it among books read for instruction, not doctrine. Some Protestant critics also noted Greek philosophical ideas (for instance the body weighing down the soul, Wis 9:15, and pre-existent souls, Wis 8:19-20) as foreign to Hebrew thought.
whyValued:
It was in the Greek Bible of the early church and very widely quoted by the Fathers, from Clement of Rome onward; the Muratorian Fragment even listed it with New Testament books. Hippo, Carthage, Trent and Jerusalem 1672 all receive it.

Catholics and Orthodox prize its clear teaching on the afterlife and the judgement of the righteous (Wis 3:1-9 is read at funerals), its doctrine of Wisdom that the Fathers read as a prophecy of Christ the Wisdom and image of God, and its passage about the righteous one mocked and killed (Wis 2:12-20), which Christians read as foreshadowing the Passion. The strong verbal parallels with Romans and Hebrews are, for them, a sign that the apostles drew on it.

title: Sirach
altTitles: Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach
language: Hebrew original; about two-thirds recovered from Cairo Genizah manuscripts (found 1896 onward), Masada (chapters 39-44) and Qumran; translated into Greek by the author's grandson in Egypt.
origin: Jesus (Yeshua) ben Eleazar ben Sira, a Jerusalem sage and teacher, writing c. 190-175 BC; his grandson's prologue dates the Greek translation to the 38th year of Ptolemy VIII Euergetes (132 BC).
summary:
Sirach is the longest wisdom book in the Bible tradition and the only one whose author is known by name. Like Proverbs it gives practical counsel on friendship, speech, money, family, work, health and table manners, but it also ties wisdom to Israel's Law: Wisdom seeks a home among all peoples and settles in Zion, and is identified with the book of the covenant (ch. 24). It ends with a long Praise of the Fathers (ch. 44-50), from Enoch to the high priest Simon son of Onias, and a closing prayer and poem.

The grandson's prologue is a precious piece of canon history: it mentions the Law, the Prophets and the other books of the ancestors, an early witness to a three-part Hebrew scripture. Sirach was quoted with respect in the Talmud, even though rabbis also ruled it outside the sacred books. The Latin name Ecclesiasticus (the church book) reflects how much Christians used it for teaching.
plain: A book of wise sayings by a Jerusalem teacher named Jesus ben Sira, about 180 BC, covering everything from friendship to money to honouring God's Law. Rabbis quoted it but did not count it as Scripture. Catholics and Orthodox do; Protestants treat it as good reading at most.

Fear of the Lord as the beginning of wisdom (ch. 1-2)

Wisdom's hymn: Wisdom dwells in Zion as the Law (ch. 24)
Praise of creation and of the famous ancestors from Enoch to Simon the high priest (ch. 42-50)
Prayer of thanks and invitation to the house of learning (ch. 51)
whyRejected:
Jews: the Tosefta (Yadayim 2.13) says the books of Ben Sira do not defile the hands, i.e. are not sacred Scripture, and the Talmud discusses whether reading it is permitted (Sanhedrin 100b). Yet it is quoted elsewhere in rabbinic literature as wise teaching, so its Jewish status is better described as respected but outside the canon. A common explanation is that it was known to be recent, written by a named sage after prophecy was believed to have ceased.

Protestants: followed the Hebrew canon and Jerome, who knew a Hebrew Sirach but still placed it outside the canon. Reformers also objected to lines such as almsgiving atoning for sins (Sir 3:30) and to the grandson's admission that his translation might fall short, which they took as an un-prophetic tone. Some Protestants also cite its harsh lines about women (e.g. Sir 25:24; 42:14) as reasons for caution.
whyValued:
Catholics, Orthodox, Ethiopians and Syriac Christians keep it. The Syriac Peshitta even translated it directly from Hebrew. It was among the books most quoted by the Fathers for moral teaching, and is listed at Hippo, Carthage, Trent and Jerusalem 1672.

Its defenders stress its antiquity (earlier than Daniel in many scholars' dating), its Hebrew original, its witness to the shape of Scripture, and its rich theology of Wisdom and the Law, which John's prologue and Jesus' invitation to the weary seem to echo. Its sayings on forgiveness anticipate the Lord's Prayer.

title: Baruch
language: Probably Hebrew for at least the first prose section (1:1-3:8); the poems may have been composed in Hebrew or Greek; survives in Greek and versions.
origin: Anonymous Jewish author or editors, attributing the book to Baruch son of Neriah, Jeremiah's scribe, in Babylon. Most scholars date it to the 2nd century BC.
summary:
Baruch is a short book in three parts, presented as a scroll Baruch read to the exiles in Babylon and sent to Jerusalem. The first part is a long prayer of confession (1:15-3:8) closely modelled on Daniel 9: Israel has sinned, the exile is just, and the people ask for mercy. The second is a poem on Wisdom (3:9-4:4) asking where wisdom is found and answering that God gave it to Israel as the book of the commandments. The third is a series of consolations to Zion (4:5-5:9), promising that her children will return.

Catholic Bibles attach the Letter of Jeremiah as chapter 6; Orthodox Bibles print it separately. Some details sit uneasily with history (Belshazzar is named as Nebuchadnezzar's son, following Dan 5, and Temple vessels are returned during the exile), which most scholars read as signs of a later, literary composition. The line that Wisdom appeared on earth and lived among people (3:37) was read by many Fathers as a prophecy of the Incarnation, though in context it refers to the Law.
plain: A short book written in the name of Jeremiah's secretary, Baruch: a prayer of national confession, a poem saying true wisdom is God's Law, and comfort for Jerusalem. Early Christian lists often counted it as part of Jeremiah. Catholics and Orthodox keep it; Jews and Protestants do not.
contents: Setting: Baruch reads the scroll to the exiles in Babylon (1:1-14)

Its confession of sin and its consolation passages are used liturgically, and the Wisdom poem is valued as a meditation on the Law as God's gift. Fathers such as Cyprian and Hilary used Baruch 3:36-38 as a testimony to Christ.

title: Letter of Jeremiah

alternatives.label: Latest likely date (before the Qumran Greek fragment)

language: Probably a Hebrew or Aramaic original; survives in Greek. A small Greek fragment (7Q2, verses 43-44) was found in Qumran Cave 7.
origin: Anonymous Jewish author writing as Jeremiah to the exiles about to be taken to Babylon; probably composed in the Persian or early Hellenistic period.
summary:
Despite its name, the Letter of Jeremiah is a single sermon of 73 verses mocking idols. Presented as a letter Jeremiah sent to the captives going to Babylon, it warns that they will see gold and silver gods carried in procession and must not fear them. In a series of refrains it argues that idols cannot speak, see, move, save themselves from fire or thieves, or help anyone, and ends that they are no gods, so do not fear them.

Its satire builds on Jeremiah 10 and Isaiah 44 and is the kind of preaching Jews needed in a world full of images. In the Vulgate and Catholic Bibles it is chapter 6 of Baruch; in Orthodox Bibles and the Septuagint it stands alone after Lamentations. Second Maccabees (2:1-3) refers to Jeremiah instructing the deportees not to be led astray by idols, which may be an allusion to it.
plain: A short sermon, written as if from Jeremiah to exiles, mocking idols as powerless lumps of metal and wood. Catholic Bibles print it as the last chapter of Baruch. Jews and Protestants do not count it as Scripture.

It is valued as a vivid, memorable teaching against idolatry that remains relevant wherever people trust in things they have made.

title: Additions to Daniel
altTitles: Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three Young Men
language: Probably Hebrew or Aramaic originals for the Prayer and Song; Susanna and Bel may have had Semitic originals, but Susanna contains Greek puns. Survive in two Greek versions (Old Greek and Theodotion) and later translations.
origin: Jewish storytellers and liturgists in the 2nd-1st century BC, adding to the Daniel tradition; place unknown (Judea or Egypt).
summary:
The Greek book of Daniel has three blocks of material not in the Hebrew-Aramaic Daniel. The Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three Young Men (68 verses) are inserted in the fiery-furnace story after Dan 3:23: Azariah (Abednego) confesses Israel's sins, an angel drives the flames out of the furnace, and the three sing a long hymn calling all creation to bless the Lord, still sung in churches as the Benedicite.

Susanna is a courtroom drama: two elders try to blackmail a virtuous wife, condemn her to death when she refuses them, and are exposed by the young Daniel, who questions them separately about which tree they saw her under. Bel and the Dragon contains two stories in which Daniel exposes the priests who secretly eat the food offered to the idol Bel, and kills a dragon worshipped in Babylon by feeding it cakes of pitch, fat and hair; he is thrown to the lions again and fed by the prophet Habakkuk, carried by an angel. Catholic Bibles number these Daniel 3:24-90, 13 and 14.
plain: Three sets of extra stories and songs in the Greek Daniel: a prayer and hymn from the fiery furnace, the story of Susanna saved from false accusers, and Daniel exposing the fake god Bel and a worshipped dragon. Catholics and Orthodox read them as part of Daniel; Jews and Protestants do not.

Song of the Three: all creation, bless the Lord (the Benedicite)
Susanna: false witness by two elders and Daniel's cross-examination
Bel: Daniel exposes priests eating the idol's food with footprints in ashes
The Dragon: Daniel kills the serpent, is thrown to the lions, and is fed by Habakkuk
whyRejected:
Jews: the Hebrew-Aramaic Daniel, including the copies found at Qumran, lacks these sections.

Protestants: Jerome translated them from Theodotion's Greek but marked them with an obelus as not in the Hebrew. In about AD 240 Julius Africanus wrote to Origen arguing that Susanna could not be authentic because Daniel's verdict depends on Greek wordplay (the mastic tree, schinos, and the verb to split, schisai; the holm oak, prinos, and to saw, prisai), which suggested a Greek original. The Reformers followed Jerome and the Hebrew text. Article VI lists the Song of the Three, Susanna and Bel and the Dragon separately.
whyValued:
The additions were part of Daniel in the Greek Bible from before Christ, and Christian art and preaching drew heavily on them: Susanna was a favourite image of the innocent saved and of the Church, and the three young men in the furnace appear in catacomb paintings. Origen replied to Africanus that the church had received these texts and that the Jews had removed passages unflattering to their elders; he also argued that puns can be imitated in translation. Hippolytus wrote the earliest surviving Christian commentary on Daniel, including Susanna.

Trent included them; the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) named Susanna and the History of the Dragon as genuine Scripture. The Benedicite is sung in Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican worship (Anglicans use it as a canticle while denying it doctrinal authority).

title: 1 Maccabees

alternatives.label: Earlier estimate (late reign of John Hyrcanus)

language: Hebrew original (lost); survives in Greek. Origen gives a Hebrew-sounding title, and Jerome said he had seen the first book in Hebrew.
origin: A Judean writer sympathetic to the Hasmonean dynasty, writing in Jerusalem around 100 BC about events of 175-134 BC.
summary:
First Maccabees is the main historical account of the Jewish revolt against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes. It describes Antiochus' ban on circumcision, Sabbath and Torah, his setting up of the desolating sacrilege on the Temple altar (167 BC), and the revolt begun by the priest Mattathias at Modein. His son Judas, called Maccabeus (the hammer), wins a string of battles, retakes Jerusalem and rededicates the Temple (164 BC), the origin of Hanukkah. After Judas dies, his brothers Jonathan and Simon combine war and diplomacy to win independence and found the Hasmonean high-priestly dynasty, ending with Simon's murder and the accession of John Hyrcanus.

Written in the style of biblical history books such as Samuel and Kings, it is sober, detailed and generally regarded by historians as reliable for events, though written to justify the Hasmonean family. Notably it never shows angels or miracles, and three times says there was no prophet in Israel at the time (4:46; 9:27; 14:41), which Protestants cite as evidence that the author himself did not see his era as one of new Scripture.
plain: A history of the Jewish revolt led by Judas Maccabeus and his brothers against a Greek king who banned Judaism, around 167-134 BC. It explains the origin of Hanukkah. Catholics and Orthodox count it as Scripture; Jews value it as history and Protestants as good reading.

Mattathias' revolt at Modein (ch. 2)
Judas Maccabeus' victories and the rededication of the Temple (ch. 3-9)
Jonathan as leader and high priest (ch. 9-12)
Simon secures independence; the people confirm him leader until a trustworthy prophet should arise (ch. 13-16)
whyRejected:
Jews: the book was not included in the Hebrew Bible; it was written after the period Jews regarded as prophetic, and its pro-Hasmonean stance may have made it less congenial to later rabbis, who told the Hanukkah story through the miracle of the oil instead. Hanukkah itself remained a Jewish festival.

Protestants: Jerome's rule (the Church reads the Maccabees for edification but not to confirm doctrine) and the Hebrew canon; the book's own statement that no prophet was then active; and a general Reformation conviction that Old Testament prophecy closed with Malachi. Article VI lists 1 Maccabees for reading.

Ethiopian: the Ethiopian canon contains three books called Meqabyan, which are entirely different works; the Greek 1-2 Maccabees are not part of the traditional Ethiopian list, hence n/a (debated: some modern Ethiopian Bibles mention them).
whyValued: It is in the Greek Bible and was counted as Scripture by Augustine, Hippo, Carthage, Trent and the Orthodox. Augustine noted that the church, not the Jews, held the Maccabees canonical because of the martyrs' endurance. Catholics and Orthodox see it as Scripture recording God's preservation of his people at a moment Daniel had foretold, and as the essential bridge between the Old and New Testaments, explaining the Feast of Dedication Jesus attended and the Jewish world of the Gospels.

title: 2 Maccabees

alternatives.label: Date of the first prefixed letter (2 Macc 1:9)

language: Greek (written in Greek, with a rhetorical, emotional style).
origin: An anonymous epitomist who condensed a five-volume history by Jason of Cyrene (2 Macc 2:23), probably in Egypt or Judea; two letters from Jerusalem to Egyptian Jews are prefixed.
summary:
Second Maccabees is not a sequel but a parallel, more theological telling of events from about 180 to 161 BC, ending with Judas' victory over Nicanor. It opens with two letters urging Egyptian Jews to keep Hanukkah, then tells of the high priest Onias, the attempt by Heliodorus to rob the Temple (stopped by a heavenly horseman), the corrupt high priests Jason and Menelaus, the persecution under Antiochus IV, and the campaigns of Judas.

Its most influential passages are theological. The martyrdom of the aged scribe Eleazar and of a mother and her seven sons (ch. 6-7) contains the clearest pre-Christian statement of bodily resurrection: the king of the universe will raise us up to everlasting life. The mother's words that God made heaven and earth not from things that existed (7:28) became a key text for creation out of nothing. In chapter 12 Judas collects money for a sin offering for fallen soldiers found wearing pagan amulets, and the author praises this because he believed in the resurrection: it was a holy thought to pray for the dead that they might be delivered from sin. In 15:12-16 the dead high priest Onias and the prophet Jeremiah are seen praying for the people. The epitomist ends modestly, saying that if his work is well done that is what he wanted, and if poorly, it was the best he could do.
plain: A more dramatic, religious retelling of the Maccabean revolt, with martyr stories and the clearest Jewish statement before Jesus that the dead will be raised. It also praises praying for the dead, which is why it became a battleground at the Reformation. Catholics and Orthodox count it as Scripture; Jews and Protestants do not.

Martyrdom of Eleazar and of the mother and seven sons; resurrection hope (ch. 6-7)

Jews: never in the Hebrew Bible; written in Greek and later than the prophetic era.

Protestants: this book was central to the Reformation dispute. At the Leipzig Disputation (1519) Johann Eck cited 2 Macc 12:43-46 in support of purgatory and prayer for the dead; Luther replied that Maccabees was not canonical and so could not establish doctrine. Calvin and the Reformed tradition added that the epitomist's apology for his style (15:38) is not the voice of the Holy Spirit, that the book praises Razis' suicide (14:37-46), and that its account of Antiochus' death conflicts with 1 Maccabees (compare 2 Macc 1:13-16 with 2 Macc 9 and 1 Macc 6). The Westminster Confession gives it no authority; Article VI allows it to be read but not for doctrine.

Catholics and Orthodox note that Hebrews 11:35 appears to allude to the Maccabean martyrs, that it was in the Greek Bible, and that Augustine, Hippo, Carthage, Trent and Jerusalem 1672 received it. They value its strong teaching on resurrection, creation from nothing, the merit of martyrdom and the communion between the living and the dead.

On 2 Macc 12, Catholics hold it shows that prayer for the dead was a Jewish practice before Christ, supporting the doctrine of purification after death; Orthodox use it to support prayers for the departed while not defining purgatory in Latin terms. They answer the modesty objection by noting that inspiration works through real human authors and styles (compare Luke 1:1-4). Augustine cited the passage in arguing that prayers for the dead are of benefit.

title: 3 Maccabees
language: Greek, in an ornate, florid style.
origin: An Alexandrian Jewish author, telling a story set in Egypt under Ptolemy IV Philopator (221-204 BC).
summary:
Third Maccabees has nothing to do with the Maccabees; the name probably came because it also tells of a pagan king persecuting faithful Jews. After defeating Antiochus III at Raphia (217 BC), Ptolemy IV visits Jerusalem and tries to enter the Holy of Holies, but is struck down after the high priest Simon prays. Back in Egypt he takes revenge: he demands that Jews register and be branded with the ivy leaf of Dionysus, offers citizenship to apostates, and rounds up the Jews of Egypt into the hippodrome to be trampled by drugged elephants.

Three times the plan fails (the king oversleeps, then forgets), and at the last moment, after the priest Eleazar's prayer, two angels appear, the elephants turn on the soldiers, and the king repents and honours the Jews, who institute an annual festival. Josephus tells a similar elephant story but under a later king, Ptolemy VIII, which suggests a shared legend. The book's concern is the fidelity and civic standing of Alexandrian Jews.
plain: A story set in Egypt about 217 BC, in which a Greek king tries to enter the Temple and then to have Egypt's Jews trampled by elephants, until God intervenes. It is called Maccabees only because of its similar theme. It is Scripture for the Orthodox, but not for Catholics, Protestants or Jews.

Simon the high priest's prayer and the king struck down (ch. 2)
Persecution of Egyptian Jews: registration, branding, the hippodrome (ch. 2-4)

Jews never received it; it is a Greek work from Egypt and was not transmitted in rabbinic tradition.

Catholics: it was never in the Latin Vulgate and is not in the lists of Hippo, Carthage or Trent, so the Western church never read it as Scripture.

Protestants: outside both the Hebrew canon and the Latin Apocrypha, so it was not even included in the Apocrypha section of Reformation Bibles. Its legendary character (elephants, the king's repeated forgetting) and duplication of a story Josephus places later also count against it historically.
whyValued:
In the Greek East, 3 Maccabees stood in many Septuagint manuscripts (Codex Alexandrinus contains it) and the Apostolic Canons (canon 85) list three books of Maccabees among the books to be revered. The Greek Orthodox churches therefore count it among the anagignoskomena (books worthy to be read); the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) did not list it separately but its Bibles include it. Some Syriac Peshitta manuscripts also contain it.

Orthodox readers value it as a story of God defending his people in the Diaspora through prayer, closely parallel in spirit to Esther and Daniel.

title: 4 Maccabees

alternatives.label: Late estimate (after the Bar Kokhba era)

language: Greek, a philosophical discourse in the style of Stoic diatribe.
origin: A Hellenistic Jew, probably in Antioch or Alexandria; Eusebius and Jerome attributed it to Josephus, which modern scholars reject.
summary:
Fourth Maccabees is a philosophical speech arguing that devout reason is master of the passions. The author first makes the case in general terms, drawing on Greek philosophy but insisting that true reason is trained by the Jewish Law. He then proves it with the examples of the martyrs from 2 Maccabees: the aged priest Eleazar, the seven brothers and their mother, who endure torture rather than eat pork.

The book expands the torture scenes in vivid detail and turns the mother into a hero greater than any philosopher. It also develops the idea that the martyrs' deaths were a ransom and an atoning sacrifice (hilasterion) for the nation's sin (6:28-29; 17:21-22), language strikingly close to how the New Testament speaks of Christ's death. It was very popular among early Christians, who honoured the Maccabean martyrs.
plain: A Jewish philosophical sermon showing that faithful reason can conquer pain and fear, using the Maccabean martyrs as proof. It speaks of their deaths as atoning for the nation. It is printed as an appendix in Greek Bibles but is not Scripture for most churches.

Historical setting: Antiochus' persecution (ch. 4)
Eleazar's debate with Antiochus and martyrdom (ch. 5-7)
The seven brothers' torture and steadfastness (ch. 8-14)
The mother's courage and death (ch. 14-17)
Their deaths as ransom; final exhortation (ch. 17-18)
whyRejected: Jews did not transmit it. Catholics never had it in the Vulgate. Protestants did not include it even among the Apocrypha. Its late date, philosophical genre (a sermon rather than history or prophecy) and the mistaken attribution to Josephus all kept it on the margins. Even in the Orthodox churches it is placed as an appendix rather than as a full member of the anagignoskomena.
whyValued:
It stands in major Greek codices (Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus) and in some Syriac manuscripts (the great Milan Peshitta codex includes it). Greek Orthodox Bibles print it as an appendix. Fathers such as Gregory of Nazianzus and John Chrysostom drew on its portrait of the martyrs, and the feast of the Holy Maccabees is kept on 1 August in both East and West.

Scholars value it highly as a witness to Jewish ideas of vicarious, atoning suffering in the decades when the New Testament was written, and to the meeting of Greek philosophy and Torah.

title: 1 Esdras
language: Greek, translated from a Hebrew-Aramaic text of Chronicles-Ezra-Nehemiah that differs from the Masoretic text in places; the contest story may have been composed in Aramaic or Greek.
origin: Jewish translator-editor, probably in Egypt in the 2nd century BC.
summary:
First Esdras retells the history from Josiah's great Passover (2 Chr 35) through the fall of Jerusalem, the return under Cyrus, the rebuilding of the Temple, and Ezra's reading of the Law (Neh 8). Most of it closely parallels canonical Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah, though in a different order and omitting most of Nehemiah's own story.

Its one large new section is the contest of the three bodyguards of King Darius (3:1-5:6): each argues what is strongest, wine, the king, or women; the third, identified as Zerubbabel, adds that truth is greatest of all and wins permission to rebuild Jerusalem. The saying that truth is great and prevails became proverbial in Latin (magna est veritas). Josephus followed 1 Esdras rather than canonical Ezra for this period. In Latin Bibles it is called 3 Esdras (Ezra and Nehemiah being 1 and 2 Esdras), which causes endless confusion of names.
plain: A Greek retelling of the end of Chronicles plus Ezra and parts of Nehemiah, with an added story of three guards debating what is strongest, won by the answer: truth. The Orthodox count it as Scripture; Catholics print it only in an appendix; Protestants list it among the Apocrypha.
contents: Josiah's Passover and the last kings of Judah (ch. 1)
Cyrus' decree and the first return; opposition to rebuilding (ch. 2)
Contest of the three guards: wine, king, women, truth (3:1-5:6)
Return under Zerubbabel and the rebuilding of the Temple (5:7-7:15)
Ezra's mission and the mixed marriages crisis (ch. 8-9)
Ezra reads the Law to the people (9:37-55)
whyRejected:
Jews: it duplicates material from the Hebrew Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah; Jews kept the Hebrew forms.

Catholics: Trent omitted it from the canon (it was not clearly distinguished in earlier lists and Jerome had not translated it). The Clementine Vulgate (1592) printed it in an appendix after the New Testament, with the Prayer of Manasseh and 4 Esdras, so that it would not be lost.

Protestants: Article VI lists it (as the Third Book of Esdras) among books read for example only; Luther left it out of his Apocrypha; Reformed churches reject it. The main objections are that it duplicates canonical books in a confused order (for example it puts the Artaxerxes correspondence before Darius) and that the contest story is a legend.
whyValued:
It was in the Greek Bible (as Esdras A, before the canonical Ezra-Nehemiah, which was Esdras B). Many scholars think the two Esdras books listed at Hippo and Carthage include it. The Orthodox read it among the anagignoskomena, and the Ethiopian church includes an Ezra book generally identified with it in its broader canon (identification debated).

It is valued as an independent witness to the text and history of the return from exile, and for its celebration of truth as belonging to God. Augustine read the contest's praise of truth as pointing to Christ, who is the Truth.

title: 2 Esdras
language: Core (4 Ezra) probably Hebrew, then Greek, both lost; survives in Latin, Syriac, Ethiopic, Georgian, Arabic, Armenian and Coptic fragments. Chapters 1-2 and 15-16 are Christian additions in Latin.
origin: The core is a Jewish apocalypse written about AD 100 in the land of Israel, in response to the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70; the outer chapters were added by Christians in the 2nd-3rd centuries.
summary:
Second Esdras in English Bibles is a composite. Its heart, chapters 3-14 (called 4 Ezra by scholars), is one of the most searching Jewish writings ever produced. Set thirty years after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem (a stand-in for Rome in AD 70), Ezra wrestles with the angel Uriel in seven visions: why does God let Israel suffer under worse sinners? Why did God not remove the evil heart from Adam? Why will so few be saved? Uriel answers that human minds cannot grasp God's ways, that the age is hastening to its end, and that the world to come is made for the few. Later visions show a mourning woman transformed into a city (Zion), an eagle (Rome) rebuked by a lion (the Messiah), and a man rising from the sea who destroys the nations with the fire of his mouth. Finally Ezra, by inspiration, dictates 94 books: 24 to publish (the Hebrew Bible) and 70 to keep for the wise.

Chapters 1-2 (5 Ezra) are a Christian prophecy of God rejecting Israel for a new people, and 15-16 (6 Ezra) are Christian oracles of woe. Chapter 7 speaks of God's son the Messiah who will reign 400 years and then die, before the resurrection. A long passage (7:36-105) about the intermediate state was missing from most Latin copies until Robert Bensly published it in 1875 from a manuscript found at Amiens.
plain: A Jewish book written about AD 100, after Rome destroyed Jerusalem, in which Ezra argues with an angel about why God lets his people suffer and why so few are saved; Christians later added chapters at the beginning and end. It is in the Ethiopian Bible and in Catholic and Anglican appendices, but is Scripture almost nowhere else.
contents: 5 Ezra: God turns from Israel to a new people (ch. 1-2, Christian)
Visions 1-3: dialogues with Uriel on evil, Adam's sin and the few who are saved (3:1-9:25)
The Messiah's 400-year reign and the intermediate state of souls (ch. 7)
Vision 4: the mourning woman becomes the new Zion (9:26-10:59)
Vision 5: the eagle and the lion (ch. 11-12)
Vision 6: the man from the sea (ch. 13)
Vision 7: Ezra restores the 24 public and 70 hidden books (ch. 14)
6 Ezra: oracles of judgement on the nations (ch. 15-16, Christian)
whyRejected:
Jews: written after AD 70 and preserved only by Christians; the rabbis did not transmit apocalypses of this kind.

Catholics: Trent excluded it; the Clementine Vulgate printed it as 4 Esdras in the appendix.

Protestants: obviously late and pseudonymous (Ezra lived in the 5th century BC), with Christian interpolations, a Messiah who dies after 400 years, and a claim that Ezra re-wrote the lost Scriptures by inspiration. Article VI lists it as the Fourth Book of Esdras for reading only; Luther excluded it.

Orthodox: absent from the Greek Bible; included as 3 Esdras in the Slavonic (Russian) Bible, so its standing is that of an appendix and is debated.
whyValued:
The Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts it (as Ezra Sutuel) in its canon. Latin Christians quoted it widely: Ambrose used it, and the Catholic liturgy for the dead borrowed its words: eternal rest grant them and let perpetual light shine on them (the Requiem introit, from 2:34-35), and the Easter-time introit about the joy of glory comes from 2:36-37.

Readers of every tradition value 4 Ezra as an honest theodicy: it lets a faithful man voice grief and protest to God, much as Job and Lamentations do, and it is a key witness to Jewish messianic hope, beliefs about Adam's sin and the afterlife in the generation of the New Testament.

title: Prayer of Manasseh
language: Greek as we have it (possibly from a Hebrew or Aramaic original). A different Hebrew prayer attributed to Manasseh was found at Qumran (4Q381).
origin: A Jewish author composing the penitential prayer that 2 Chronicles says Manasseh prayed; first attested in the Christian Didascalia Apostolorum (3rd century).
summary:
This fifteen-verse prayer is put in the mouth of King Manasseh of Judah, the most wicked king in Kings, who according to Chronicles was taken to Babylon in chains, humbled himself and prayed, and was restored. The Chronicler mentions that his prayer was recorded in the records of the seers, and this text fills that gap.

It moves from praise of the Creator who bound the sea, to the confession that God has appointed repentance for sinners, to a deeply personal confession (I have sinned more than the number of the sands of the sea; I bend the knee of my heart), and ends with a plea for forgiveness and a promise of lifelong praise. It is one of the finest penitential prayers in Jewish and Christian literature, and is used in Orthodox Great Compline and as an Anglican canticle.
plain: A short, moving prayer of repentance written in the name of King Manasseh, the worst king of Judah, who the Bible says repented in exile. It fills in the prayer that 2 Chronicles mentions but does not quote. Most churches value it for devotion, but few count it as Scripture.
contents: Praise of God the Creator, before whom all tremble (v. 1-5)
God's mercy has appointed repentance for sinners (v. 6-8)
Confession: sins more numerous than the sand (v. 9-10)
I bend the knee of my heart: plea for forgiveness (v. 11-13)
Promise of praise all the days of life (v. 14-15)
whyRejected:
Jews never received it; its first attestation is in a Christian church order.

Catholics: Trent did not include it; the Clementine Vulgate printed it in the appendix.

Protestants: Article VI lists it among the Apocrypha, and Luther printed it as the last book of his Apocrypha; Reformed churches reject it. The reasons are its late attestation, absence from the Hebrew Bible, and the fact that it is a composition supplying a prayer Scripture only mentions. Some Protestants also note that the Chronicles account of Manasseh's repentance is absent from Kings, so the prayer builds on a debated episode.

Orthodox: it is among the Odes appended to the Psalter in Greek Bibles and used liturgically; its formal status is sometimes described as appendix rather than full deuterocanon (debated).
whyValued: It is valued almost everywhere as a model of repentance and of God's mercy toward the worst of sinners. The Didascalia and the Apostolic Constitutions quote it in full to show bishops how to receive penitents. Codex Alexandrinus includes it among the Odes. The Ethiopian church includes it within its Chronicles. It is prayed in Orthodox Compline and was placed among the canticles of the Church of England.

criteria.note: Old Testament-era prayer; apostolicity does not apply.
Probably 2nd-1st century BC, first attested in the 3rd century AD.
Classic biblical theology of sin, repentance and mercy.
Used devotionally across many churches but formally canonical in few.
Prayed in liturgy (Orthodox Compline, Anglican canticles).
Presented as Manasseh's own prayer; most scholars regard this as a literary attribution.

title: Psalm 151
altTitles: Psalm of David outside the number
language: Hebrew original, now attested in the Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran Cave 11 (11Q5, column 28); also Greek, Syriac, Latin, Ethiopic.
origin: A Jewish poet writing in David's voice; the Greek version is a condensed combination of two Hebrew psalms.
summary:
Psalm 151 is a short autobiographical poem in David's voice, labelled in the Septuagint as written by David himself and outside the number (of the 150 psalms). David says he was small among his brothers and a shepherd; his hands made a harp; God sent his messenger and anointed him rather than his handsome brothers; and he went out against the Philistine, cut off his head with his own sword and removed reproach from Israel.

Until 1956 it was known only in translation. The Psalms Scroll from Qumran then revealed a longer Hebrew original, actually two psalms (151A on David's anointing and 151B on Goliath), which the Greek had compressed. The same scroll contains other non-canonical psalms (numbered 152-155 in Syriac Bibles), showing that the outer edge of the Psalter was still fluid in some Jewish circles around the time of Jesus.
plain: A short psalm in which David remembers being the youngest shepherd brother, chosen and anointed by God, and defeating Goliath. It sits at the end of the Greek, Syriac and Ethiopian Psalters, and a Hebrew form was found in the Dead Sea Scrolls. Orthodox and Ethiopians read it; Jews, Catholics and Protestants do not.
contents: David the youngest, shepherding his father's sheep
His hands make an instrument; he gives glory to God
God sends his messenger and anoints him above his brothers
He kills the Philistine giant with his own sword and removes Israel's shame
whyRejected:
Jews: the Masoretic Psalter has 150 psalms; this one was outside it (as even the Greek title concedes).

Catholics: it was not in Jerome's Latin Psalters as a canonical psalm and was not considered at Trent, so it never entered the Catholic canon (status n/a).

Protestants: outside both the Hebrew Bible and the Latin Apocrypha, so it was not even part of the Apocrypha debate.
whyValued:
Psalm 151 is in the Septuagint Psalter in major codices (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus) and so is read in Orthodox Bibles. The Syriac Psalter includes it with Psalms 152-155, and the Ethiopian Psalter includes it. The Qumran discovery shows it had a genuine Hebrew pre-history, which raised its standing among scholars.

It is valued as a meditation on God choosing the small and overlooked, a theme close to the heart of the Bible.

title: 1 Enoch

alternatives.label: Astronomical Book and Book of Watchers (oldest parts)

language: Aramaic original (eleven fragmentary manuscripts at Qumran cover every section except the Parables); survives complete only in Ge'ez (classical Ethiopic), with Greek portions.
origin: A collection of five Jewish works written between about 300 BC and the turn of the era, in the land of Israel, attributed to Enoch, who walked with God (Gen 5:24).
summary:
1 Enoch is really a small library of five books. The Book of Watchers (ch. 1-36) expands Genesis 6:1-4: angels called Watchers, led by Shemihazah and Asael, descend, marry women, teach forbidden arts, and father giants whose violence brings the Flood; Enoch tours heaven, the places of punishment and the ends of the earth. The Parables or Similitudes (37-71) describe a heavenly figure called the Son of Man, the Chosen One and the Messiah, who will sit on the throne of glory and judge kings. The Astronomical Book (72-82) sets out a 364-day solar calendar. The Dream Visions (83-90) include the Animal Apocalypse, retelling Israel's history with animals for people up to the Maccabean revolt. The Epistle of Enoch (91-108) warns the rich and promises reward to the righteous.

Enoch was widely read by Jews before AD 70 and by early Christians. The New Testament letter of Jude quotes it directly (Jude 14-15 = 1 Enoch 1:9), and 1-2 Peter seem to know its story of imprisoned angels. Lost to the West for centuries, it was brought to Europe from Ethiopia by James Bruce in 1773 and first translated into English by Richard Laurence in 1821.
plain: An ancient Jewish collection written in Enoch's name, telling how rebel angels corrupted the world before the Flood, describing heaven, a coming judge called the Son of Man, and the end of evil. The New Testament letter of Jude quotes it. It is Scripture only in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.
contents: Book of Watchers: fall of the angels, the giants, Enoch's heavenly journeys (ch. 1-36)
Parables: the Son of Man and the judgement of kings (ch. 37-71)
Astronomical Book: the 364-day calendar (ch. 72-82)
Dream Visions: the Animal Apocalypse of Israel's history (ch. 83-90)
Epistle of Enoch and Apocalypse of Weeks (ch. 91-108)
whyRejected:
Jews: although Enoch was popular at Qumran and in Second Temple Judaism, rabbinic Judaism did not receive it; it was attributed to a pre-Flood figure (so it could not have been written down and preserved through the Flood, as some argued), it promoted a solar calendar against the Temple's lunar one, and its angel-centred apocalyptic world fell out of favour after AD 70.

Christians (Catholic, Protestant, Orthodox): after early enthusiasm, the Fathers doubted it. Augustine said it could not be proved genuine because of its extreme antiquity and that the Jews did not accept it, so it should not be trusted even if it contained some truth. Jerome reported it was counted among the apocrypha. Its angel-marriage story was rejected by those who read Genesis 6 of Seth's line. That Jude quotes it was taken to mean only that Jude used a true saying, as Paul quoted Greek poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12).
whyValued:
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church received 1 Enoch with its Bible from earliest times and has preserved the only complete text. For them, Jude's quotation of Enoch as one who prophesied confirms its standing, as did its use by early Fathers.

Early Christians valued it: the Epistle of Barnabas cites Enoch as Scripture, and Tertullian argued it should be accepted, noting that Jude quotes it. Today scholars of every tradition value it as essential background to the New Testament: its Son of Man, its picture of fallen angels bound until judgement, Gehenna, and the coming judgement all shed light on Jesus' teaching and the apostles' letters.

title: Jubilees
altTitles: Apocalypse of Moses (in some ancient references)
language: Hebrew original (about fifteen copies at Qumran); survives complete only in Ge'ez, with Latin, Greek and Syriac fragments.
origin: A priestly Jewish author in Judea in the mid-2nd century BC, close to the circles that produced the Qumran community.
summary:
Jubilees retells Genesis 1 to Exodus 12 (and the Sinai setting of Exodus 24) as a revelation given to Moses on Mount Sinai by an angel of the presence, who dictates from heavenly tablets. History is organised into periods of 49 years (jubilees), and the whole runs fifty jubilees from creation to the entry into Canaan.

The author fills gaps (names of Adam's daughters and Noah's wives, Abraham rejecting his father's idols), smooths moral difficulties, and above all shows that the patriarchs already kept the Law: Sabbath, festivals, purity and a 364-day solar calendar that he insists on against a lunar one. He forbids intermarriage and nakedness (a reaction to Greek gymnasium culture), and gives a strong role to angels and to Mastema, chief of evil spirits. The Qumran Damascus Document refers to it as an authority.
plain: A retelling of Genesis and early Exodus, presented as what an angel revealed to Moses on Mount Sinai, showing the patriarchs already keeping the Law and a 364-day calendar. It was popular at Qumran. Only the Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts it as Scripture.
contents: Prologue: Moses on Sinai receives the history from the angel of the presence (ch. 1)
Creation and the Sabbath (ch. 2)
Adam to Noah; the Watchers and the Flood (ch. 3-10)
Abraham's rejection of idols and his covenant life (ch. 11-23)
Jacob, Levi's priesthood and Joseph (ch. 24-45)
Moses, the Exodus and the Passover; Sabbath laws (ch. 46-50)
whyRejected:
Jews: rabbinic Judaism followed the lunar calendar Jubilees condemns, and it did not accept a second Sinai revelation alongside the Torah. Its sectarian flavour (shared with Qumran) made it unacceptable to mainstream post-70 Judaism.

Christians: never part of the Greek or Latin Bibles; Fathers such as Epiphanius and Jerome knew it as an apocryphal Little Genesis. Its claim to be dictated to Moses and its legal rigour made it of limited Christian interest outside Ethiopia.
whyValued:
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church received it as canonical Scripture and preserved its only complete text. Ethiopian readers value its strong Sabbath and festival theology and its harmony with their Enoch tradition and calendar concerns.

Scholars of all traditions value it as one of the most important examples of rewritten Bible, revealing how Jews around 150 BC read Genesis and the debates over calendar, Law and Gentile culture that shaped the Judaism of Jesus' day.

criteria.note: Not apostolic; presented as Mosaic but generally regarded as pseudonymous.
Mid-2nd century BC, contemporary with Daniel in many datings.
Monotheistic and Torah-centred; its calendar and Law-before-Sinai claims are distinctive.
Canonical only in Ethiopia; important at Qumran.
Read at Qumran and in Ethiopia; little use elsewhere.
Claims dictation by an angel from heavenly tablets to Moses.

language: Greek as we have it; Jewish sources in Aramaic and Hebrew lie behind parts (the Aramaic Levi Document and a Hebrew Naphtali text were found at Qumran).
origin: Disputed: either a Jewish work of the 2nd-1st century BC later edited by Christians, or a Christian composition of the late 2nd century AD drawing on Jewish traditions. Either way the present form is Christian.
summary:
Modelled on Jacob's blessing of his sons (Gen 49), this work gives the deathbed speech of each of Jacob's twelve sons. Each patriarch tells his life story, confesses a besetting sin or celebrates a virtue, gives moral teaching, and predicts the future of his tribe. Reuben warns against sexual sin (recalling Bilhah), Simeon against envy, Judah against drunkenness and greed, Joseph praises chastity (Potiphar's wife) and brotherly love, Issachar commends simplicity.

Two recurring ideas stand out: love for God and for one's neighbour as the summary of the Law (strikingly close to Jesus' double commandment), and a coming salvation from the tribes of Levi and Judah, priest and king. Several passages plainly speak of God becoming man and of the Gentiles' salvation, which shows Christian hands. Robert Grosseteste's Latin translation (1242) made it popular in medieval Europe.
plain: The farewell speeches of Jacob's twelve sons, each warning against a sin or praising a virtue and predicting the future. It contains strikingly Christian-sounding lines, because Christians edited or wrote it. It is not Scripture in any major church, though it was popular in the Armenian church and the Middle Ages.

whyValued: It was read widely as moral teaching: medieval Christians treasured it as an ancient Jewish witness to Christ, and Grosseteste believed the Jews had hidden it because of its prophecies. Modern scholars value it for the Jewish ethics it preserves (on sexuality, envy, anger and love of neighbour) and for the debate it raises about how Jewish texts were Christianised.

title: Psalms of Solomon

alternatives.label: Earliest psalms (after Pompey's capture of Jerusalem)

language: Hebrew original (lost); survives in Greek and Syriac.
origin: Pious Jews in Jerusalem, often linked with Pharisaic circles (debated), reacting to the Roman general Pompey's capture of Jerusalem in 63 BC and the failures of the Hasmonean rulers.
summary:
These eighteen psalms, attributed to Solomon, lament the Roman conquest of Jerusalem. They describe a foreign conqueror (clearly Pompey) breaching the walls, entering the sanctuary, and later being killed on the shores of Egypt, and they blame the disaster on the sins of Jerusalem's own leaders who usurped David's throne (the Hasmoneans). The righteous accept God's discipline; the sinners will perish.

Psalms 17 and 18 contain the fullest pre-Christian portrait of the Davidic Messiah: a son of David who will purge Jerusalem of Gentiles and sinners, shepherd the people in righteousness, smash the arrogant like a potter's jar with an iron rod, destroy enemies by the word of his mouth, and be called the Lord Messiah. They are crucial for understanding what many Jews hoped for when Jesus was hailed as Son of David.
plain: Eighteen psalms written after the Romans captured Jerusalem in 63 BC, mourning the city and hoping for a righteous Son of David, the Messiah. They show what many Jews expected of the Messiah in Jesus' time. No major church counts them as Scripture.

In the Greek Christian world they were sometimes copied with the Bible: the table of contents of Codex Alexandrinus lists them after the New Testament with 1-2 Clement, and the Stichometry of Nicephorus lists them among disputed books (antilegomena). They never became canonical, hence rejected (in the sense of disputed and not received) for the Greek tradition, and n/a elsewhere.
whyValued: Some Syriac Bible manuscripts transmit them alongside the Odes of Solomon. Scholars value them highly as a dated witness (63-48 BC) to Jewish piety and messianic hope just before Jesus, to the idea of the righteous suffering discipline, and to the Pharisee-era debates about the Temple and the Hasmoneans.

title: 2 Baruch
language: Probably Hebrew original, then Greek (a few Greek fragments survive); complete only in one Syriac manuscript (the 6th-7th century Codex Ambrosianus in Milan); the closing letter circulated separately in many Syriac Bibles.
origin: A Jewish author in the land of Israel writing a generation after the Roman destruction of the Temple in AD 70, using the Babylonian destruction as a mask.
summary:
2 Baruch is a twin of 4 Ezra, written in the same years and wrestling with the same catastrophe. Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, sees angels dismantle Jerusalem's walls and hide the Temple vessels before the Babylonians enter, so that the enemy cannot boast. He laments, fasts and receives visions: a period of twelve woes, then the Messiah's revelation, when Behemoth and Leviathan will be food for the righteous and the earth will yield ten-thousandfold; the resurrection, in which the dead rise in their old form to be recognised and then are transformed; and a vision of dark and bright waters summarising history.

Unlike 4 Ezra, Baruch is more confident: the Law remains, and Israel must keep it. He ends with a letter to the nine and a half tribes in exile urging faithfulness. A famous line insists on personal responsibility: Adam is the cause only for himself; each of us has become our own Adam.
plain: A Jewish book written about AD 100 after Rome destroyed the Temple, in which Jeremiah's scribe Baruch mourns, receives visions of the Messiah and the resurrection, and urges Israel to keep the Law. Only one complete copy survives, in Syriac. No church counts it as Scripture, though its closing letter was copied in Syriac Bibles.

whyValued: In the Syriac church the Letter of Baruch (chapters 78-87) was copied in Bible manuscripts as a biblical book, and the whole apocalypse is in the great Milan Peshitta codex alongside 4 Ezra and 4 Maccabees. Scholars value it for Jewish beliefs about the resurrection body, the Messiah, the Law and human responsibility in the era when the Gospels and Paul's letters were being read.

title: Assumption of Moses (Testament of Moses)

alternatives.label: Original composition in the Maccabean crisis, updated later
Final form after Herod's death (4 BC)

language: Hebrew or Aramaic original (lost), then Greek (lost); survives in one incomplete 6th-century Latin palimpsest found in Milan and published by Antonio Ceriani in 1861.
origin: A Jewish author in Judea in the early 1st century AD (possibly reworking a Maccabean-era text), writing as Moses' farewell to Joshua.
summary:
The surviving text is Moses' farewell to Joshua before his death. Moses hands Joshua secret books and predicts Israel's history: the conquest, the division of the kingdom, the Babylonian exile, the return, wicked priests and kings, a powerful insolent king (clearly Herod the Great) who will rule 34 years, and his sons who will rule for shorter times. A persecution follows, during which a Levite named Taxo and his seven sons resolve to die rather than break the Law. Then God's kingdom appears, the devil is ended, and Israel is exalted to the stars. The manuscript breaks off as Joshua despairs and Moses reassures him.

Ancient writers mention an Assumption (or Ascension) of Moses that told of the archangel Michael disputing with the devil over Moses' body. Origen and others said this was the source of Jude 9. Most scholars think the lost ending of our Testament of Moses, or a related work, contained that scene, though the exact relation between the Testament and the Assumption is debated.
plain: Moses' farewell prophecy to Joshua, retelling Israel's history up to Herod and the coming of God's kingdom. Ancient writers say a book like this told of the angel Michael and the devil arguing over Moses' body, which the letter of Jude mentions. It is not Scripture in any church.

The fact that Jude alludes to a tradition it contained was explained, as with Enoch, as Jude using a known story to make a point, not endorsing the whole book.

Scholars also value its view of history, its portrait of Herod's era from a pious Jewish perspective, and Taxo as a model of martyrdom expecting God to avenge.

title: Ascension of Isaiah
language: Greek original (only fragments survive); complete only in Ge'ez (Ethiopic), with Latin, Slavonic and Coptic parts.
origin: Christian prophetic circles of the late 1st or early 2nd century, probably in Syria or Palestine, possibly using an older Jewish story of Isaiah's martyrdom.
summary:
The first half (chapters 1-5) tells how King Manasseh, under the influence of the demon Beliar and a false prophet, has Isaiah sawn in two with a wooden saw; Isaiah dies steadfast, speaking with the Holy Spirit. Embedded in it is a Christian prophecy of the Beloved's coming, the apostles, the church's decline, and Beliar's appearance as a matricidal king (Nero).

The second half (chapters 6-11) is Isaiah's vision: an angel leads him up through the seven heavens to see God, the Beloved and the angel of the Holy Spirit worshipping. He then sees the Beloved descend secretly through the heavens, taking the form of each level's angels so as not to be recognised, be born of Mary in Bethlehem (with an unusual painless birth account), be crucified, descend to the dead, and rise and ascend in glory. It is one of the earliest Christian texts outside the New Testament on the hidden descent of Christ and the Trinity.
plain: A Christian work in two parts: the story of the prophet Isaiah being sawn in half by King Manasseh, and Isaiah's vision of travelling through seven heavens and seeing Christ come down secretly to be born, die and rise. It survives complete only in Ethiopic. It is not part of any official canon, though it is valued in Ethiopia.

whyRejected: Jews did not transmit it (though the rabbis knew a tradition that Manasseh killed Isaiah). Church writers grew suspicious of it: Jerome and Epiphanius report that it was used by heterodox groups (such as the Archontics and Hieracas), and its docetic-sounding descent of Christ in disguise and its distinctive angelology seemed unorthodox. It was therefore listed among apocrypha in the West and East.
whyValued: Ethiopian Christianity preserved it and values it as a revered writing (some lists of the broader Ethiopian canon include it; its formal status is debated). Scholars value it as early evidence for Christian prophecy, belief in the Trinity, the virgin birth, Christ's descent to the dead, and Nero-as-antichrist traditions. The Martyrdom story is the most likely source of the tradition that Hebrews 11:37 alludes to.

title: Apocalypse of Abraham
language: Probably Hebrew original, translated into Greek and then Old Church Slavonic; survives only in Slavonic manuscripts (14th century and later), partly within the Palaea Interpretata.
origin: A Jewish author writing after the Temple's destruction in AD 70, probably in the land of Israel; some passages may be Christian or Bogomil additions.
summary:
The first part tells how young Abraham, working in the idol shop of his father Terah, realises the idols are powerless: one breaks, another burns, and he concludes that the true God must be the creator. God calls him, and his father's house is burnt with fire from heaven.

The second part expands the covenant sacrifice of Genesis 15. Guided by the angel Yahoel, who bears God's name, Abraham ascends on the wings of the sacrificial birds to the heavenly throne, sees the fiery chariot and the creation below, and is shown a picture of the world divided between Israel and the nations. The fallen angel Azazel, who tempted Adam and Eve, tries to deter him. Abraham sees the Temple destroyed and is told of a future judgement and of an elect one who will gather the people. Its throne-chariot vision is an early example of Jewish mystical traditions.
plain: A Jewish book from about AD 100 in which Abraham first sees through his father's idols, and then, guided by an angel, rises to heaven and sees God's throne, the history of the world and the Temple's destruction. It survives only in Old Slavonic. No church counts it as Scripture.

whyValued: Scholars value it for early Jewish throne-mysticism, angelology (Yahoel bearing God's name, Azazel as Satan figure), and for Jewish reflection on the destruction of the Temple. It also preserves the popular story of Abraham rejecting idols, also found in Jubilees and later rabbinic midrash (Genesis Rabbah 38).

title: Life of Adam and Eve
language: Greek (Apocalypse of Moses) and Latin (Vita) are the main versions; also Armenian, Georgian and Slavonic. A Hebrew original has been proposed but is unproven.
origin: Disputed: either a Jewish work of the 1st century AD or a Christian composition from Jewish traditions; it circulated in many church communities in different forms.
summary:
This family of texts tells what happened to Adam and Eve after Eden. In the Latin version they repent by standing in rivers, Eve in the Tigris for 37 days and Adam in the Jordan for 40, but Satan, disguised as an angel of light, deceives Eve again. Satan explains his hostility: when Adam was created in God's image, Michael commanded the angels to worship him, and Satan refused and was cast out.

As Adam nears death, Eve and Seth travel to Paradise to ask for oil from the tree of mercy, but Michael tells them it will be given only at the end of time. Eve tells her children the story of the Fall. Adam dies, angels intercede, and God takes his soul to Paradise in the third heaven, promising resurrection. The tale shaped medieval legends such as the Holy Rood (wood from Eden's tree becoming the Cross) and has close parallels in the Qur'an's account of Iblis refusing to bow to Adam.
plain: Stories about Adam and Eve after leaving Eden: their repentance, Satan's second trick, why Satan fell (he refused to honour Adam), and Adam's death and promised resurrection. It exists in several languages and versions. It was never Scripture, but it influenced Christian art, legend and even the Qur'an.

title: Letter of Aristeas
language: Greek.
origin: An Alexandrian Jew writing as Aristeas, a Gentile courtier of Ptolemy II Philadelphus (285-246 BC), to his brother Philocrates.
summary:
This is the earliest account of how the Torah came to be translated into Greek, the beginning of the Septuagint. Aristeas says that Demetrius of Phalerum, the royal librarian, urged Ptolemy II to obtain the Jewish Law for the Alexandrian library. The king freed Jewish slaves, sent lavish gifts to Jerusalem, and the high priest Eleazar sent 72 elders, six from each tribe. After a week of banquets in which they answer the king's questions on government and virtue with wisdom, they translate the Law on the island of Pharos in 72 days. The Jewish community approves the translation and pronounces a curse on anyone who alters it.

Along the way Eleazar gives an allegorical defence of the food laws (clean animals teach justice and gentleness), and there is an idealised description of Jerusalem and the Temple. Historians doubt many details (Demetrius probably did not serve Ptolemy II), but agree the Torah was translated in Alexandria in the 3rd century BC. Later writers embellished the story so that the translators worked separately and produced identical texts, a miracle Jerome rejected.
plain: A story, told by a supposed Greek courtier, of how 72 Jewish scholars translated the Law of Moses into Greek for King Ptolemy's library in Alexandria. It is the origin of the name Septuagint (the Seventy). No one ever treated it as Scripture, but it shaped how Jews and Christians viewed the Greek Bible.

whyValued: It explains the origin and authority of the Septuagint, the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and of the New Testament writers. Philo and Josephus retold it, and Christian Fathers (Justin, Irenaeus, Augustine) used expanded versions to argue that the Greek Old Testament was divinely inspired. That belief became one of the main arguments for the wider (Septuagint-based) canon. Jerome, by contrast, dismissed the legend of separate cells and preferred the Hebrew.

title: Community Rule
language: Hebrew.
origin: The Yahad (community) associated with Qumran on the Dead Sea, widely identified with the Essenes; found in Cave 1 in 1947 with ten more copies in Cave 4.
summary:
The Community Rule is the founding charter of a Jewish sect that withdrew from the Jerusalem Temple, which it considered polluted, to live in strict purity by the Dead Sea. It describes the annual covenant ceremony with blessings and curses, the admission of members through stages of testing over two years, shared property, communal meals and study, and a penal code (for example, penalties for falling asleep in the assembly or speaking foolishly).

Its Treatise on the Two Spirits teaches that God created a spirit of truth and a spirit of falsehood, light and darkness, that struggle in every person until the final visitation. The community saw itself as a living temple whose prayer and obedience atone for the land, and it applied Isaiah 40:3 (prepare in the wilderness the way of the Lord) to its study of the Law, the same verse all four Gospels apply to John the Baptist. It expects a prophet and the messiahs of Aaron and Israel.
plain: The rule book of the Dead Sea Scrolls community, explaining how members joined, shared property, prayed and were disciplined, and teaching a struggle between light and darkness. title: War Scroll
altTitles: War of the Sons of Light against the Sons of Darkness
language: Hebrew.
origin: The Qumran community or related circles; found in Cave 1 in 1947 with further fragments in Cave 4.
summary:
The War Scroll is a detailed plan for the final war between the Sons of Light (Israel's faithful, especially the sect) and the Sons of Darkness (Belial's forces, the nations, and especially the Kittim, probably the Romans). The war will last forty years with sabbatical rests, in seven phases: three times the light will prevail, three times darkness, and in the seventh God's mighty hand will win.

Much of the scroll reads like a military manual with a priestly overlay: the sizes and inscriptions of banners and trumpets, the formations of the infantry and cavalry, the ages of soldiers, and the priests who sound the trumpets and pray. The archangel Michael leads the angelic army alongside Israel. It is a vivid example of how some Jews before Jesus expected the kingdom of God to come through holy war.
plain: A battle plan for the final war between good and evil, written by the Dead Sea Scrolls community, with banners, trumpets, priests and angels fighting alongside the faithful. It shows how some Jews expected God's kingdom to come by war. It was never Scripture for anyone.

It is listed here as an example of the many texts found in the Dead Sea caves that were valued by one group but never part of anyone's Bible.
whyValued: It shows the vocabulary of light and darkness, Belial, and Michael's war in heaven that also appears in the New Testament, and helps readers see what was different about Jesus' and the apostles' teaching: their war is not against flesh and blood, and the Lamb conquers by his death. It is also a major source for understanding Jewish expectations of the Roman threat.

title: Book of Jasher

alternatives.label: Collection completed in Solomon's time or later

language: Hebrew (presumably a collection of poetry).
origin: An early Israelite collection of heroic songs, probably compiled during the early monarchy; known only by name and two or three quotations.
summary:
The Bible twice quotes a Book of Jasher (Hebrew Yashar, upright). Joshua 10:13 cites it for the poetic command, Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and Moon, in the Valley of Aijalon. Second Samuel 1:18 says David's lament over Saul and Jonathan (How the mighty have fallen) was written in it. The Greek text of 1 Kings 8:53 also cites a Book of the Song for Solomon's dedication words, and many scholars think this is the same book with two Hebrew letters swapped (shir, song, for yashar). It appears to have been an anthology of national poetry honouring Israel's heroes.

The original is lost. Several later books have borrowed the name and should not be confused with it: a Hebrew midrash Sefer ha-Yashar printed in Venice in 1625 (a medieval retelling of Genesis to Judges, translated into English in 1840 and reprinted by Latter-day Saints and others), and an English forgery of 1751 by Jacob Ilive claiming to be translated by Alcuin. Neither is the ancient book.
plain: A lost collection of ancient Israelite poems that the Bible quotes twice, for the sun standing still and for David's lament over Saul and Jonathan. The books sold today as the Book of Jasher are later works, one a medieval Jewish retelling and one an 18th-century forgery. The original is gone.
contents: Poem on the sun and moon standing still at Gibeon (quoted in Josh 10:12-13)
David's lament for Saul and Jonathan, the Song of the Bow (quoted in 2 Sam 1:19-27)
Possibly Solomon's words at the Temple dedication (Greek 1 Kgs 8:53)
whyRejected: It was not rejected; it was lost. The biblical writers treated it as a respected source, the way a historian cites an older anthology, not as Scripture itself. Nothing suggests any community kept it as a holy book. The modern books bearing its name are not the original and are rejected as Scripture by all mainstream traditions.
whyValued: Its value lies in what the quotations show: biblical authors used and named sources, and Israel had a tradition of written heroic poetry earlier than the books we have. Christians and Jews alike see no loss to the Bible's sufficiency, since what God wished to preserve was taken up into the canonical text.
